There was also a lot of online chatter about Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered's November release date. How was that release date chosen? Is that date sticking?

Strange: I mean, yes. This is a key thing, really. November 3 is Godzilla's birthday. That's Godzilla day. That's the day that's when Toho releases new Godzilla films in Japan. That's the day that new Godzilla announcements are made. I mean, that's Godzilla Day, and I didn't know that 25 years ago when I first started working at Pipeworks. Now, I'm like, "Well, obviously, we should come out on Godzilla Day." I think that's great. People who are big Godzilla fans, they see that it's coming out November 3, and they're like, "Oh, I see what they're doing." Because they know that's Godzilla Day. Now we know, so we want to show that off.

So, that leads into my next question: You are still looking at November for Godzilla's birthday because you have to.

Strange: Absolutely. We have to. Yeah.

One of the reasons there has been so much talk online – and I have loved seeing all of the memes and light-hearted jokes around it – is if you look at the video game release calendar for the year, Godzilla is one of the very, very few games coming out in November. I'm not an expert, but my guess is that Grand Theft Auto 6 has something to do with that. I've seen Pipeworks tweet about this a few times too, so my question is: Why isn't Godzilla scared to go up against GTA 6?

Strange: I have also loved all those memes. I think that's great. Honestly, wasn't even in our head at all when we were picking the release date.

That's not my business. I make the video games. I'm not too worried about when they come out. If Atari had come to us and said, "Wow, we can't because we think it's going to affect the sales with GTA," we would've had that discussion. But no one ever said anything. It was like, November 3 is obviously the day. Based on when we started, when we got the contract with Atari, we were like, how long does it take to manufacture the physical disc? Yeah, November was always the date.

So, the GTA thing, that's hilarious. It's really cute memes. We've all really enjoyed that. It was never part of our thinking. I wasn't looking at that calendar and being worried in any way or thinking about what other games are coming out because the Godzilla fans are very excited for it. They'd buy it on any day that it came out, and putting it on Godzilla's birthday, that's just respectful.

https://t.co/Lh4c0SyWvl pic.twitter.com/4hzmDYUVVy

— 🐙Dumbo Octopus🐙 (@DumboOctopus4) June 7, 2026

https://t.co/cUmNKjwGBD pic.twitter.com/fBWjeJ2AoR

— TheColeBrew (@TheColeBrew) June 6, 2026

Was there any temptation to include even more monsters in the roster? Obviously, as the series went on, there were more.

Strange: Sure. There were possibilities of doing all kinds of different things. We talked about a lot of different plans. We had the ability, now, to bring in assets from these old Pipeworks games, so what do we do with that? It wasn't obvious that a remaster of the first game was the thing. We talked through a lot of different plans, but a faithful remaster of the first game is the plan that we settled on. So, that's the way we're going, but certainly before we settled on that plan, we talked about doing different things. We talked about doing different sets of things, or what can we do now that we have this technology? Do we make a new game? I mean, all kinds of things were on the table, but the plan we settled on was a faithful remaster of the original game, so that means using the original cast.

The number one thing I see people asking for is, now that Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee is coming back, they obviously want the other games. Is that a desire that the team has seen, and is it something you would be interested in bringing to life at some point?

Strange: Let me tell you, I had that desire long before we announced this game, so I get it. I want to do all that stuff, too. I mean, all that stuff is now technically possible. We can bring all those assets from all those Spigot games, and we can bring them into Unreal, and we can do all kinds of things with that. The unfortunate, bland answer is that it depends on what kind of a contract we put together. Pipeworks as a company is really big now. When we were doing these games back 25 years ago, we were literally 12 people in one room. Now, Pipeworks is like 300 people. I mean, it is huge. We are working on dozens of different projects. We have all kinds of different stuff pulling at our time and attention, and there are all kinds of different possibilities for what we're doing at any given time.

Atari has their own ideas and their own plans. Me, as an individual person, I love the idea of bringing all that content back to the players. I think that's great. I would especially love – and I'm speaking a little out of turn here – but I would love to avenge the sort of mediocre release of Godzilla: Unleashed.

There was a lot of trouble on that, and I had a conversation where we were like, 'Would we remaster every possible game?' I was like, "Nobody wants a straightforward remaster of Godzilla: Unleashed because that game was busted in some ways." So, if we wanted to revisit that content, I'd want to do it better. There is not already a contract for that, but whatever. Contracts… We've got a whole biz dev section, Atari's got a whole biz dev section, they're talking based on the response… I mean, a lot of stuff is on the table. There's a lot of conversations to be had in the future, and I'm very excited for all of that.

I'm definitely rooting for it. This goes back to my earlier question: Was there any temptation to build on the original game with content from the more modern Godzilla releases? Minus One, Shin Godzilla, or even the Monsterverse series? These, essentially, could even be skins for Godzilla. Is that something you considered, as well?

Strange: The Monsterverse, no. That is a separate entity. Godzilla Minus One, Shin Godzilla, Godzilla Minus Zero, that stuff is Toho, though. So, that is something that has been sort of discussed in the ether. That is something that's a little interesting. There's also been a lot of discussions about what is a skin? What's a new character? How much do you need to differentiate things?

There was a lot of discussion since the game's release about which characters are too similar to other characters. I know a lot of that is good-hearted, but man, some of that stabs at me because this is my area. I'm building the combat, the movement, the controls; I'm differentiating the characters. When I made the first game, we had Godzilla '90s and Godzilla 2000, and in my mind, that was Ryu and Ken. I was like, "Oh, yeah, so they're basically the same because they're rivals." Then people said, "Oh, they're just clones of each other and so lazy." I was like, "It's Ryu and Ken!"

Where people would be like, "Ghidorah and Mecha-King Ghidorah, they're just clones." I would say, "They're so different. They're so different. They have totally different weaknesses. Yes, they're sharing many animations, but…" Anyway, that sort of stuff really bugged me. You can see in the later games, I worked really hard to make it super clear that all the monsters are really different. They've got really different play styles and strategies. That was the part for me in this remaster that has been the hardest. It's all the stuff I'm like, "This is the part where it's the same, but people want them to be different, but I can't because it's got to be the same. It has to be the same game. I can't make it more different."

Godzilla 2000 runs faster than Godzilla '90s, but it's like 9% faster. It's a small difference. I was like, "Maybe I'll make that bigger." Nope, it's got to be the same. Every time I want to make it even more different or expand on things, I was like, "It's got to be the same," but let's talk about the one big exception because I assume you're going to. Do you want to ask the question about the one big exception about being the same?

I do know about bringing in the alternate Mechagodzilla design, so enlighten me!

Strange: Yes, that was the big change. Instead of using the '93 Mechagodzilla mesh, we're using a 1975 Mechagodzilla mesh, and that was not an initial plan. When we first sat down and we started, we were like, "It's going to be a faithful remaster. That's the plan." I was like, "OK, faithful – but what do we want to change?" I came up with a short list of things that we are changing, even though it's a faithful remaster.

Then, we got into development, and we're going through, and we're working stuff, and it just came up, and as soon as it came up, it was so obvious. We were building all the new character meshes, and we were getting to the point where we were going to build the Mechagodzilla mesh, and it was said out loud: "Obviously we should change."

In the original game, we didn't know we were making more than one game. We thought this was it. We didn't think there was going to be a bunch of others and remakes. So, we're like, "Mechagodzilla's got to be a character." We're making this game, and the '93 Mechagodzilla – which, that movie didn't come out in the U.S. until '94 – that's like five years old. That was the most recent Mechagodzilla. We were like, 'We'll use that. That's Mechagodzilla.' That's the one we had toys for that was easy to get. In fact… [Editor's Note: Strange held up a small Mechagodzilla figurine.] This is the actual toy that Pipeworks bought that we modeled our Mechagodzilla off of. These are all the original toys, and I love it when people say things like, "The characters, they look like they're modeled off these toys." Yeah, they absolutely are. We bought a set of these toys, and that's how we did it.

So, that's Mechagodzilla, but then we were like, "What does a Mechagodzilla do?" Well, we weren't exactly matching the '93 film. We were just pulling all the Mechagodzilla stuff together to make our sort of a gestalt Mechagodzilla. The same way with Ghidorah; it wasn't Ghidorah from 'this film.' We were just pulling in lots of different Ghidorah elements. Kiryu didn't even exist. When we were making the game, that movie hadn't even been shot. Then, for the Japanese version, they're like, "Oh, we want to add this new Mechagodzilla." Kiryu wasn't even the fan name. It was the New Mechagodzilla. We called it Mechagodzilla 2000 or Mecha 2K.

So, inside the game files, there's Mechagodzilla and Mecha 2K, but then, we said, "Well, this is confusing because what do we call him? We can't call him that." We then called it Mechagodzilla 2 for the '93 version, and then Mechagodzilla 3 for Kiryu. But then, I hadn't thought about this: In the Showa era, '74 is Mechagodzilla, and then '75 is the same Mechagodzilla, but on his armband, it says MG and then MG2. Well, that implies that the '75 is Mechagodzilla 2. So, then what? So, '93 is now Mechagodzilla 3, but he's in a different continuity. The naming is so bad. I hate it so much. What do you call it? Is it Mechagodzilla 2K is 3, but now it's 4?

And all the file names are all just all over the place. What we say in-game, and what we've recorded for the announcer voice, is just different in different games. I was like, "Oh, my God. Let's tamp it down." Mechagodzilla is the '74/'75 character. Super Mechagodzilla is the '93 character. Kiryu is the 2002 character. Three different names. Given that was the naming and given that the announcer says Mechagodzilla, we were like, "We're using the '74/'75. That's what we're doing." We had to then go to Atari. In fact, we did this without getting Atari's approval. We did it, and we were like, "Look what we did, Atari, please say it's OK!" Atari said, "This is cool, but we have to go to Toho now and talk to them and get permission," and thankfully they did.

Toho said, "Yes, well, as long as there's an accurate Mechagodzilla, that's all good. It's all kosher." It would've been no big deal if we had called that out before the project started, like, "Here, it's on the list of changes," but it was midstream. As we got to the point where we had to make the character match, we were like, "We should fix this to fix the naming and fix..." So, that was a big deal. I'm so pleased. I'm so pleased we got that done.

I, alone in my office, cheered. I was so happy to see that revealed. That's the main thing I saw everybody talking about online after the trailer came out.

Strange: So, we did this internally. I showed it off to one of the artists who's a big Godzilla fan, and he fell off his chair. We were just on a Zoom call. It's late at night. He just fell out. I said, "This is going to be so good." Still, though, it's the same game. It plays exactly the same. He's got the rocket fingers; he's got the jet thrusters. It's all exactly the same. It's the cross-attack beam instead of the plasma cannon, but it functions just the same, the same hit boxes. It has different VFXs; the same laser eyes, but the laser eyes are now rainbow. But mechanically, it's all exactly the same. We didn't change anything; we just changed the mesh. The collision spheres are all exactly the same. The animations are the same, et cetera.

Is Mechagodzilla 2 not in the game, then? Completely replaced?

Strange: Yes, we have a single character. The character's name is Mechagodzilla, which is the original character name we used in the first game, but the visual appearance of that is the 1975 Mechagodzilla.

Is there anything you're particularly excited for fans of the original game to see in this remaster?

Strange: Yeah. Gosh, there are things I'm very excited about. There are some things that we were trying to do an announcement of or show off. Yeah. OK. Bear with me.

We have a director mode. You can pause the game and fly the camera around, pause time, zoom in, and use that to do screenshot sort of stuff, turn off the HUD... I think that's going to be awesome. I think we'll see a lot of people making videos and taking screenshots and capturing content in that way. I think that's going to be really cool. I think people are going to like that a lot. We had that as a debug option in the original game, but it wasn't something we shipped out to the consumers. This time, we put a little time into it and made a little UI, so we let people have that. I think that's going to be great.

Let's see… We also have the new unlock system. It's been talked about a little bit, but that's my baby. I really like it a lot. I think it's a lot more interesting, a lot more engaging. The original unlock system was kind of a grind and a little dull, and we didn't tell you how to unlock anything. It's like you only have three characters of 12. You're like, "Well, what do I do?" It was like, "I don't know. Figure it out." Now, there's a whole research system, there’s rumors, you're sort of playing as the G-Force labs. It's like, "Rumors of a sighting of a monster over here. Maybe we should go investigate that."

We use that to say, "Play a different game mode. Play some Melee games, play an Adventure game, play some Survival games." All these different things lead you to different unlocked paths, and then as you play the game, you earn research points that you then use to unlock the monsters.

I played through recently, and I unlocked Orga first. I want Orga first; Orga is the first one I went after, and I did it. This is nitpicky: The press release says "unlock things in any order." That's not 100% true. Some things have to happen after other things, and there are some natural things. Like, Orga takes a lot more research than Godzilla 2000. Most people, I think, will get Godzilla 2000 before they get Orga, but you don't have to. You can do it in another order, but it's not literally any order.

Two of the characters, they have prerequisites of having another character unlocked first, but it's really flexible. I think it's a lot of fun. I love just restarting and getting a clean save and unlocking and trying to figure out how it can be more efficient. It's like, "Oh, now I have to play four games in San Francisco." Yeah, I think that's a lot of fun. I nerd out on that stuff a lot, but again, it's my system.

On the flip side of that, hopefully, a lot of new people will pick up this game, as well. People who have never played it, who are fans of Godzilla, or maybe even people who've just seen the recent movies. What's your pitch to newcomers on why they should play this game? Why this is a great Godzilla experience?

Strange: I mean, I think the game is really fun. We have some playtester videos that came back recently, and there were these people who were trying to be really harsh about the game and really nitpicky, or whatever. But I had video, and they were just laughing and just cackling as they would play, and it was so much fun. Sometimes, people get down the nuance, and it's like, well actually, the game is quite complicated. There's actually a lot of nuance on different block heights, and there are five different attack directions, and there are 12 different damage types. There's all this nuance. It's like, yeah, but also, boom, boom, boom, I shot you with my high-energy breath, and it's awesome.

I really enjoy fighting games. I play a lot of fighting games, but I think that fighting games are often built in kind of a mean-spirited way. In most fighting games, if I hit you, you can't do anything. If I keep hitting you and keep hitting you, you just can't do anything. In some ways, in the way that people often approach fighting games, if I play really well, you literally don't get to play the game. I'm hitting you all the time because I'm really good, and you're like, [noises of frustration]. You never get to play the game. I think that's really unfun, so all of these games have always been built to not be that way. I don't know. If I'm really good, I'm going to hit you, bam, but then you get knocked away, and you stand up, and you can just come right back and hit me back.

A rank beginner playing these games should be able to take away half of my health before I win. Even if you aren't very good at the game and don't understand the systems, you should be throwing down lots of damage, getting lots of hits in. You should be playing the game a lot. I think that's something that makes it really fun, is that everyone's always engaging. You get to be a big monster, you get to smash the city, you get to send your opponents flying, you get to charge up your high-energy breath. All that stuff is exciting and fun, and I think people like those one-on-one combat fighting games, but especially when they actually get to play it. We made a game here where everyone really gets to play the game all the time, and especially you get into four-player and everyone gets to play the whole time. I think that's really fun and very special.

What does the power of modern consoles allow you to do for this game? Are there any console-specific features? Obviously, the PlayStation has a touch pad, for example. I don't know if that's something you utilized or anything like that.

Strange: We did not use the touch pad, specifically. We thought about it. I'm really into controllers and different control things. One thing we did use that we worked hard to make sure worked really well is that, on the Switch, we made sure that you could play the game with a single Joy-Con because local, in-person multiplayer is, I really think, where this game shines. I think about being a kid, and if I had a Switch, I don't necessarily have other controllers – but the Switch has got two. So, here, I take it out, and I can play with my sister. I want to be able to have a controller, and we can just sit there and play. It's better if you have the full controller or the Pro Controller, whatever. It's better, but it's very playable with a single Joy-Con.

That's important because man, I want kids to be able to say, "You and I each have a Switch. We can play four-player because we have two Switch consoles; that's four controllers. Four people can now play the game." I thought that was really important. Part of the reason that this game was originally a GameCube game and not an Xbox game is because the GameCube had four ports. It had four controller ports, and Atari was always like, "This is a four-player game. It's a party game. It's a melee game. That's so important." Being able to have four people locally and play is really important, so supporting the single Joy-Con, I think, hopefully, will really drive Switch 2 owners to play in local mode. I think that's going to be big.

We obviously talked a lot about maintaining the roster and keeping the roster the same, but there is one character that I have heard rumors about. I'm not sure I've seen official confirmation about it, but there was talk about a PlayStation 2 port that may have had Baragon included.

Strange: Yes.

Did you want to bring Baragon into the Remaster? Is that something you considered?

Strange: No. So, that's true; The Baragon files exist. We have all that stuff, but Baragon was never finished.

In order to finish Baragon, I'd have to bring in new animators. I'd have to bring in new audio. We'd have to create a bunch of new data that didn't exist before. Obviously, we did create Baragon for the second Godzilla game. People think of them as similar, but we did not use a single thing from the first Godzilla game in the second Godzilla game. It is 100% built from scratch. It's the same people with the same ideas, but the skeletons are different. The animations are different. The whole combat system is different. So, yeah, we do have Baragon assets that were built for Godzilla 1, but we don't have a complete set, so there was never any possibility of bringing that over.

Maybe the second biggest question I've seen so many people talk about is, there were some Xbox exclusive maps and locations. Is that something we can expect to see in the remaster, or are those locked onto that system?

Strange: I'm not going to answer that question at this time.

Did you know that you were making a game that would stick with so many people back in the 2000s? And is that same special sauce, I guess you could say, in this Remaster, in your opinion?

Strange: We definitely didn't know. Pipeworks had worked on a thing, a thing and a half, before this, but Godzilla was the first console game that Pipeworks actually published, finished, and it was not clear. I mean, just very briefly, Pipeworks was working on a thing, started to staff up, and then that fell apart, and they had to let their staff go. Then, they had this Godzilla; it was a backup sort of thing that was going, and they said, "Well, maybe the Godzilla thing is actually going to happen."

I was the first person hired to staff them up for that Godzilla project, so it was really just founders and me making this Godzilla thing. It was not clear that we were going to succeed. Maybe this whole Pipeworks thing wasn't going to succeed. They'd lost a project. It was like, "We had to let people go. If this Godzilla thing doesn't go, that's it. We close up shop." We were definitely scrambling. We weren't like, "Let's make it really good." We were just… we were in survival mode, for sure.

OH MY GOD https://t.co/oXAT8nNNN6

— 💥 GODZILLA DAMM REMASTER COMING NOVEMBER 3 💥 (@GodzillaNewGame) June 6, 2026

I mean, I had a young child, and I was like, "I really want to keep making these video games." I'd moved back to [Eugene, Oregon] to join Pipeworks, and I was like, "This is very exciting, but we got to really hit this one." I'd say, really quickly, once we launched it, we knew that we had something really good, and that was really exciting going into making all the future games and making [Rampage: Total Destruction].

That was very exciting. This was a discussion that I had with Pipeworks’ chief technology officer Dan White. We were talking about this initial thing, and he was like, '"Well, how do we know it's going to have that same feel? How are we going to get the feel? Where does that feel come from? That's a hard thing to do." I was like, "Dan, I'm right here. I know exactly how to get the team to reproduce the original feel, because the original game feel was a deliberate goal, not some unintended accident." I'm the combat and controls and monster guy. I said, "That's my focus. I promise you, we're going to get it," and we did. So, that feels really good.

Is there anything else you'd like to add about Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered, Pipeworks, Godzilla in general, or anything like that?

Strange: I'd say I really like working in Pipeworks. I think Pipeworks is a great place. I've been really lucky to be able to work here for so long. It's a lot of fun. They've got this great Godzilla room that they made for us, and we were doing screenings of Godzilla films at the theater down the street with the team. That's great to have that sort of support. I'm really pleased that Toho and Atari want to keep going with this. I know when you're a fan, you're just like, 'Make the thing that I want,' but there's a lot that goes into it. There are a lot of decisions, a lot of things that have to line up to make these things happen, and it's great when they line up, and we should always be thankful when projects work out and line up.

I did want to say one other change we made to the game. Here we go. Your exclusive announcement: We have cut Hedorah from the game.

Oh, wow.

Strange: Because I always hated it. I hated it. It was in the plan. Like, 'Hedorah sometimes shows up as a stage hazard.' In the original game – a lot of people may only vaguely be aware – Hedorah, the Smog Monster, sometimes, 25% of the time, would just randomly be in a level. He was just flying around in his little flying blob form – couldn't even see it – except that it would cut your energy regeneration down to 20% of normal. In the original game, one quarter of the time, your energy regeneration just doesn't work, and you don't know why. Why is that? It's like, "Hedorah is there." I was like, "Is he? I can't see." Sometimes, if the camera's just right, it'd be like, "What was that blob?" I didn't know that. We didn't tell you that. We didn't indicate it.

It was super hard to see. Do you know who Hedorah is? Why is it there? Then, if you could shoot your beam and hit Hedorah – which you can't because you can't even see it – it was terrible. It was a terrible system. It was, like, a quarter of the time the game is a lot less fun. That was on the list. That was the number one thing on the list when we were remaking the game. It was like, "Yeah, we're cutting that because that was stupid.'" Just make the game less fun sometimes. No, no. So, there we go. We have cut Hedorah from the game.

I definitely remember having that same experience when I was younger, being like, "Where's my power? I have no idea what's going on," and then eventually learning. That's hilarious that Hedorah got cut.

Strange: Yeah. Yep. Kill it with fire. No fun. No fun at all.

Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN. He's best known for his work at sites like The Pitch, The Escapist, and OnlySP. Be sure to give him a follow on Bluesky (@mikecripe.bsky.social) and Twitter (@MikeCripe).

items.title: Xbox Acknowledges 'Major Outage' as Sign-In Issues Hit PC and Consoles [UPDATED]
items.description: Microsoft has resolved a "major outage," which saw account issues across PC, Xbox Series X/S and other devices.
items.author: Tom Phillips
items.content:
UPDATE: Microsoft has said it's now addressed the issues that caused an Xbox services outage earlier today, bringing players back online.

"Great news, everyone! Engineering has confirmed mitigation," reads a new post on the Xbox Support social media account. "Signing in or creating an account should be back to normal now. We appreciate the heads-up — keep them coming if anything else pops up."

All in all, the issue appears to have been resolved within six hours.

ORIGINAL STORY: Microsoft has acknowledged a "major outage," with account issues across PC, Xbox Series X/S, and other devices.

If you're struggling to log into your Xbox account in order to play games, you're not alone. Numerous reports of issues have popped up this morning, and Microsoft itself has now acknowledged the problem.

Describing the incident as a major outage, the Xbox Support page for the issue explains that impacted users "may not be able to sign-in to your Xbox profile, may be disconnected while signed in, or have other related problems."

Meanwhile, "features that require sign-in like most games, apps and social activity won't be available." Impacted platforms include Xbox Series X/S, Xbox One, Xbox 360, Xbox on Windows, Android, iPhone, Cloud and web services.

Microsoft initially acknowledged the issue at 5.:09am ET today, and is still working on the issue some four hours later. As yet, there's no word on the reason behind the outage.

We are aware that some users are encountering errors when attempting to sign in or create an account. Thank you for your patience while we investigate this issue. We'll update as soon as we have more — keep an eye on https://t.co/MGxnmqdcis.

— XBOX Support (@XBOXSupport) September 2, 2026

items.title: Viral Gaming Toilet Chair Appears to Resurface Via Facebook Marketplace — Listed as in 'Used' Condition for $500
items.description: A viral fan-made Fortnite toilet chair made infamous via TikTok has apparently resurfaced via Facebook Marketplace, with the item priced at $500 and listed as in "used" condition.
items.author: Tom Phillips
items.content:
A viral fan-made Fortnite toilet chair made infamous via TikTok has apparently resurfaced via Facebook Marketplace, with the item priced at $500 and listed as in "used" condition.

The so-called "Battle Bucket" was the subject of a now-deleted 2023 TikTok video from user @usecodelitty200iq, who explained the home-made contraption was the reason he could "play Fortnite for so long without going to the bathroom."

The Battle Bucket is essentially a flip chair with a crude hole cut into the seat, and an orange 5-gallon Home Depot bucket underneath. A curved length of piping has also been placed at the front of the seat, arcing down into the bucket's base. On the back of the chair, a G Fuel sticker has been artfully placed.

"I call this the Fortnite Battle Bucket," @usecodelitty200iq described at the time. "It has two holes. One for going number one, and another for going number two," he continued, pointing to the pipe and seat hole in quick succession.

@xset The Battle Bucket Is CRAZY.. 😂 (TT:@/usecodelitty200iq) #foryoupage #foryou #fyp #trending #gaming #fortnite ♬ original sound - XSET

While the original video has now been removed, numerous examples of it remain online via reuploads. And now, the device itself appears to have resurfaced for real, via an X account that supposedly spotted it listed on Facebook marketplace. Certainly, the listing includes a high-quality photo of the Battle Bucket not part of the original video, suggesting whoever is behind it has access to the real thing.

"I've had this for a few years and used it almost daily," the listing reads. "Has been thoroughly cleaned and works beautifully." And then, one final note: "Real offers only! No lowballs I know what I got."

**USED** Battle Bucket ($500) pic.twitter.com/ff2nqoCN6t

— insane facebook marketplace items (@insanemrktplace) August 31, 2026

As a functioning replacement for going to the bathroom, or indeed a replacement for operating as a functional human being, this seems unlikely to raise $500. As a piece of internet history, well, it still seems unlikely to raise $500. And although the listing claims the viral chair has been cleaned, I'd still be worried of a different kind of viral issue when sitting down on it.

Here's hoping we hear more on the Fortnite Battle Bucket, if and when the sale proceeds. In the meantime, the internet has certainly been having its fun with the listing, with comments from various brands piling in.

"Powered by yours truly," wrote the official G Fuel social media account. "It's been an honor to serve you 🫡."

"Adding this to the list of banned items at LAN," wrote UK esports event organiser Epic.LAN.

I also enjoyed this oil painting of the Fortnite Battle Bucket, immortalizing its TikTok appearance forever:

I made an oil painting of the most insane Facebook marketplace find pic.twitter.com/rzkm4gPHoL

— Cayde.wav (@caydeplanet) September 1, 2026

Let us know if you're planning to bid on the item, or indeed if you become the, er, lucky owner.

Image credit: X/TikTok/@usecodelitty200iq, Epic Games

items.title: Pokémon Fans Think the Franchise's New TCG Movie Hides a Secret Mega Evolution
items.description: The reveal of upcoming movie Pokémon: Wild Card hid a brand new Mega Evolution in plain sight, fans believe.
items.author: Tom Phillips
items.content:
The reveal of upcoming movie Pokémon: Wild Card hid a brand new Mega Evolution in plain sight, fans believe.

Over the weekend, the 2026 Pokémon World Championships included a flurry of new Pokémon announcements, including the first new Pokémon movie for seven years. Due to launch in theaters next year, Pokémon: Wild Card will feature a TCG player "battling and striving to be a champion," accompanied by a mysterious Mimikyu.

Of course, Mimikyu does not currently have a Mega Evolution — not in the series' original Pokémon X and Y batch of Megas, or in the fresh menagerie introduced last year via Pokémon Legends: Z-A. But there is something odd about the Mimikyu in that poster — do you see it?

Yes, the Mimikyu is glowing with rainbow-colored light — a very similar rainbow-colored light to the effect of Pokémon as Mega Energy, used to Mega Evolve. Is it a coincidence, or something more? And if we are about to see a Mega Mimikyu revealed, when could it debut in video game form?

One popular suggestion is that Mimikyu will evolve in next year's Pokémon Winds and Waves, the franchise's long-awaited 10th generation of games due to arrive exclusively for Nintendo Switch 2. With these games and Pokémon: Wild Card arriving around the same time, this would be a neat teaser — and certainly, anime movies and series have previously featured various Pokémon debuts before they're actually available in-game.

One other avenue for release could be via a final update to Pokémon Legends: Z-A, a game which focuses squarely on Mega Evolution. This would likely make more sense thematically, and there's been no suggestion that Winds and Waves will include Mega Evolution themselves. Indeed, as a new generation of games, the upcoming titles are more likely to feature their own regional mechanic (such as Gigantamax in Sword and Shield, or Terrestrialization in Scarlet/Violet).

Could Mega Mimikyu debut sooner rather than later in Legends: Z-A, as a way to tide fans over while news on Winds and Waves' launch window remains thin on the ground? Or could this all just be another one of Mimikyu's tricks? Fans seem convinced Mega Mimikyu is coming, either way.

— 👑🤴🏻Spoopy🪦💀 (@Prince_Spoopy) September 1, 2026

Mega Mimikyu incoming?? https://t.co/rAu2VWlyZq

— Moxie✨✏️ (@Moxie2D) August 31, 2026

bet on mega mimikyu https://t.co/2aYhRo88DI

— abeo (@CassidyCrpKilla) August 31, 2026

For everything announced during the 2026 Pokémon World Championships and PokémonXP, check out our roundup. Pokémon Tales: The Misadventures of Sirfetch'd and Pichu was announced back in 2025, but news about the series streaming on DisneyXD and more was revealed during a panel at this year's PokémonXP.

items.title: LEGO PlayStation Images Leak, Revealing Some Incredible PS1 Easter Eggs
items.description: The long-rumored LEGO PlayStation set has been glimpsed in leaked photos, and it's an impressive recreation of Sony's retro console with a several great Easter eggs.
items.author: Tom Phillips
items.content:
The long-rumored LEGO PlayStation set has been glimpsed in leaked photos, and it's an impressive recreation of Sony's retro console with a several brilliant Easter eggs.

Earlier this year, product listing leaks pointed to a LEGO PlayStation console coming this October. And now, with a month to go, the first photos of the set have hit the internet.

Reliable LEGO source Brick Tap has revealed images of the set's box, as reportedly found in a LEGO store. It's still unclear when LEGO will make the set official, though perhaps we'll hear more tomorrow, during Sony's next State of Play broadcast. That's due to stream online at 9am Eastern, on September 3.

The set itself will reportedly contain 1,911 pieces and come with a pricetag of $160. There will also reportedly be an Astrobot gift with purchase, available while stocks last.

72306 PlayStation first look (via Brick Tap)
by u/BrickTap in Legoleak

While there's no images yet of the Astrobot add-on, the main set's box shows the LEGO console and controller. Printed brick elements perfectly recreate the DualShock's iconic Square, Triangle, Circle and Cross buttons, and the pad can also plug into the console's front.

The console itself includes the PS1's flip-up disc tray, while its sides pull away to reveal miniature scenes from Ape Escape and Gran Turismo. It's a very cool touch, and one that's reminiscent of the Easter eggs found in LEGO's Nintendo range, such as the diorama's hidden in its 1-UP Block set.

It likely won't be long until Sony and LEGO make the set official, and it joins a growing range of retro console builds — such as the Nintendo Entertainment System below. Last month, LEGO also revealed a refreshed range of Super Mario sets, now scaled to feature the first Nintendo minifigures.

Will you be adding the LEGO PlayStation to your gaming LEGO collection?

items.title: Eight-Player Splitscreen Added to Mario Kart 8 Deluxe
items.description: Nintendo has conjured up an eight-player splitscreen mode for Mario Kart 8 Deluxe, available now in a free update on Switch 2.
items.author: Luke Reilly
items.content:
Mario Kart fans with more than three friends rejoice: Nintendo has conjured up an eight-player splitscreen mode for Mario Kart 8 Deluxe on Switch 2. The free update is available now.

The mode carves up the usual four-player split one more time, resulting in eight portrait-style windows.

You’ll just need eight controllers and enough seating for you and seven rivals. Or perhaps you just need to win or place to make it onto the couch, and all the losers will just have to sit on the floor?

Nintendo also notes Mario Kart 8 Deluxe players on Switch 2 will be able to utilise ‘CameraPlay’, which adds your friends’ faces on screen as you race them.

The update also comes with enhanced visuals and brings shorter load times.

Mario Kart 8 Deluxe recently earned a well-deserved spot in IGN’s 30th anniversary round-up of racing game masterpieces. If you too feel the need for speed, feel free to check out what other iconic and acclaimed racers made the list.

items.title: Star Wars Zero Company Was Originally Pitched as a Titanfall Universe Game
items.description: Star Wars Zero Company was originally pitched as a game in the Titanfall universe.
items.author: Cade Onder
items.content:
Star Wars Zero Company was originally pitched as a game in the Titanfall universe.

As part of a larger report on Star Wars Zero Company, Game File's Stephen Totilo uncovered a lot of interesting details about the game's development. The big headline was that the bulk of the studio was furloughed just weeks before launch as Bit Reactor ran out of money, but there's hope that those employees will be brought back following the game's success. However, there is one other bit that caught some eyes: Zero Company wasn't initially imagined as a Star Wars game.

Game File dug up legal documents pertaining to a lawsuit between Bit Reactor leadership which paints a picture of Zero Company's development. Director Greg Foertsch worked with studio co-founder Alison Kelly to develop pitches for a tactics game, which eventually landed a meeting with Respawn Entertainment co-founder Vince Zampella. The late gaming executive asked Foertsch to make a pitch based on Respawn's own IP, which would've meant the game would be connected to the Titanfall universe.

Game File notes the pitch was directly linked to Apex Legends, which is set in the Titanfall universe, but it's unclear if the signature mechs would've returned or if it would've been rooted in the hero characters from Apex Legends, similar to the upcoming Rainbow Six Tactics game. Zampella ultimately rejected the pitch for the Titanfall universe tactics game and instead told the team to try again, this time with the Star Wars IP, which Respawn has a heavy hand in.

Respawn are the creators of the Star Wars Jedi games and also worked on a scrapped FPS Star Wars game, so it's no surprise that they'd be interested in expanding that IP with other genres. And as fate would have it, Star Wars Zero Company was born. The game has been one of the biggest surprises of 2026, garnering rave reviews and an impressive concurrent player count on Steam. Over the weekend, the game peaked at 77,889 on Steam and has had strong word of mouth across social media.

Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

items.title: Stanley Kubrick’s Daughter Responds to Eyes Wide Shut Conspiracy Theories
items.description: Stanley Kubrick’s daughter Vivian has addressed rumors surrounding Eyes Wide Shut, debunking claims that key scenes were removed after the director's death.
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
Vivian Kubrick, the daughter of the late director Stanley Kubrick, has addressed conspiracy theories about her father’s final film, Eyes Wide Shut, conspiracies spread, in part, a few years ago by podcaster Joe Rogan and his guest, filmmaker Roger Avary.

“You know, this is as good a time as any to finally address the missing 20 minutes from Eyes Wide Shut. It’s a story that has been circulating for many years, so let me tell you what I actually know and don’t know. For context, my father always had his outtakes incinerated once a film was finished, specifically to prevent the studio from later re-editing his work or creating alternative versions. There has been a lot of speculation that some 20 minutes were removed from Eyes Wide Shut after he died,” Kubrick posted on X.

“This will be very disappointing to many people, but I certainly did not hear anything about a missing 20 minutes at the time, nor have I heard anything since that would confirm such a section ever existed. I guess you could stop reading right here,” Kubrick continued, clarifying she wasn’t in “a position to know everything that may have happened before or immediately after my father’s death” as she was in Los Angeles to score a movie at the time.

EYES WIDE SHUT: THE MISSING 20 MINUTES

You know, this is as good a time as any to finally address the missing 20 minutes from Eyes Wide Shut. It’s a story that has been circulating for many years, so let me tell you what I actually know and don’t know.

For context, my father… pic.twitter.com/hsgllDKJnV

— Vivian Kubrick (@ViKu1111) September 1, 2026

“The only alteration I heard about at the time was the use of CGI—computer-generated figures—to obscure some of the nudity in the orgy scene, which Warner Brothers wanted in order to secure an R rating for the film. But I did not hear that any shots or scenes were removed,” Kubrick wrote.

“When my father died, Eyes Wide Shut had reached picture lock and was moving through the final stages of post-production. It had just been shown to the studio heads, I assume with a temporary music track, while the final sound mix and some of the music work were still to be completed. This was 1999, in the era of physical film distribution.”

As Kubrick explained, Eyes Was Shut was edited on Avid, a process that didn't include any “permanent digital archive people imagine today.” After further elaborating on the negative creation and editing process of the time, Kubrick added, “I have no knowledge of whether any of the Avid editorial material from the production still exists.”

Cont.
University of the Arts London. They hold the official archive of my father’s surviving papers, production materials and other records, spanning his entire career, including Eyes Wide Shut. But to my knowledge, there is no surviving cache of Avid rushes from the film.

So… pic.twitter.com/5Zr3hzSWkI

— Vivian Kubrick (@ViKu1111) September 1, 2026

Kubrick suggested the University of the Arts London might know more as they “hold the official archive of my father’s surviving papers, production materials and other records, spanning his entire career, including Eyes Wide Shut. But to my knowledge, there is no surviving cache of Avid rushes from the film.

“That is as far as I can honestly go. I never heard of a missing 20 minutes at the time, I have never subsequently seen or been shown any evidence that such a section existed, and I know of no surviving material that establishes that it did,” Kubrick posted.

“I cannot tell you what may or may not have happened during the 30-some hours immediately after my father’s death; I was not there. But unless substantive evidence emerges—and I do not regard stories from certain people who, in my opinion, are inventing them after the fact as evidence; people often want to sensationalize their part in a story, if indeed they even had a part—the story that 20 minutes were removed from Eyes Wide Shut after his death remains, to my mind, an actual conspiracy theory, not an established fact.”

After mourning her father, Kubrick said she “involved myself very closely in protecting my father’s work and took that responsibility extremely seriously” and said she would have found out about any missing footage from Eyes Wide Shut had it existed.

Curiously, Kubrick ended her posts with a slew of hashtags about the Epstein Files and tagging podcasters Joe Rogan, Alex Jones and Julian Dorey. In his December 2024 podcast with Rogan, Avary not only claimed there was 20 minutes of missing footage from Eyes Wide Shut but that its original ending was altered by Warner Bros.

Sitting opposite Quentin Tarantino during the podcast, Avary claimed, citing "second hand" knowledge, the studio changed the original ending over Kubrick’s objections – only for the filmmaker to die a few days later.

Avary also claimed Eyes Wide Shut was originally meant to end with Tom Cruise and Nicole Kidman’s characters giving their child away to a “pedo cult,” which suggested Stanley Kubrick, in 1999, may have somehow been aware of Jeffrey Epstein’s sex trafficking crimes involving the rich and powerful years before they were publicly exposed.

Avary maintained the “party line” about Eyes Wide Shut is that the theatrical release is Kubrick’s intended version - even Nicole Kidman has stated that’s the case – but that it’s clear to him that the studio meddled with the film after Kubrick died.

Warner Bros. has long maintained that the film they released is Kubrick’s version.

After mourning her father, Kubrick said she “involved myself very closely in protecting my father’s work and took that responsibility extremely seriously” and said she would have found out about any missing footage from Eyes Wide Shut had it existed.

Curiously, Kubrick ended her posts with a slew of hashtags about the Epstein Files and tagging podcasters Joe Rogan, Alex Jones and Julian Dorey. Avary maintained the “party line” about Eyes Wide Shut is that the theatrical release is Kubrick’s intended version - even Nicole Kidman has stated that’s the case – but that it’s clear to him that the studio meddled with the film after Kubrick died.

Warner Bros. has long maintained that the film they released is Kubrick’s version.

items.title: CD Projekt Red Boss 'Isn't Worried' About Delays for Next-Gen Consoles as RAM Prices Soar
items.description: CD Projekt Red joint CEO Michał Nowakowski opened up about the developer’s reaction to the rising price of consoles and the possibility of next-generation hardware getting delayed.
items.author: Virginia Glaze
items.content:
CD Projekt Red joint CEO Michał Nowakowski opened up about the developer’s reaction to the rising price of consoles and the possibility of next-generation hardware getting delayed due to RAMaggedon.

Speaking with The Game Business in a September 1 interview, Nowakowski said he’s “not worried” about console costs potentially affecting sales of CDPR’s titles.

“Consoles are still necessary to broaden the audience on the casual or semi-casual level. It’s important to have [something] easy to plug in and enjoy gaming,” he told the outlet. “I'm a big believer that they’re going to weather the storm. Pricing is the objective challenge. And the rumors... we hear them about the next gen being delayed. I don’t know if they’re true.”

He’s not very fussed about this possibility, either. For him, how CDPR reaches gamers is “a little irrelevant” — it’s the content that matters most, regardless of how it gets in players’ hands.

“Content is the king. And if the content is right, people will find a way to play it,” Nowakowski explained. “When we launch, if PS5, Xbox Series X/S is what people are playing, we’re going to be there. We’re going to find a business model that’s going to work for us, that’s going to be fine for players, and that’s it.

“If you ask the dev team, they will always answer: ‘Give us as much power as you can, because we want to show off the best stuff.’ That’s the way they’re wired. But they’re realistic. If the next-gen gets delayed, it could be the case that some ideas are put on a shelf for the future. We’d have to adjust. We’re not worried on the commercial side. Consoles are here to stay.”

This last bit is what’s raising eyebrows among fans. With PlayStation making the sweeping decision to end production of physical game discs starting January 2028, many are worried that consoles will eventually go the way of the Dodo if other big brands like Xbox or, God forbid, Nintendo, follow suit.

But CDPR, at least, is confident that consoles will stick around as long as gamers want to use them — and that seems to be the case, at least judging by players' overwhelming reactions to PlayStation’s vision for an all-digital future.

CDPR has been on gamers’ good side lately, notably stepping in to help an indie game dev whose equipment was stolen at gamescom by offering to send “a few things” his way.

The developer is also making sure to provide physical goodies for gamers who want to buy The Witcher 4, even if it releases after PlayStation’s game disc cutoff date.

items.title: GTA 6's Morality Meter Will Reportedly 'Shatter' and Make You Irredeemable If You Cause Too Much Mayhem
items.description: Grand Theft Auto 6's morality meter can reportedly "shatter" and lead to you becoming essentially irredeemable for an entire playthrough of the game.
items.author: Cade Onder
items.content:
Grand Theft Auto 6's morality meter can reportedly "shatter" and lead to you becoming essentially irredeemable for an entire playthrough of the game.

YouTuber TGG got to see GTA 6 behind closed doors during a recent preview and has provided a ton of details on the game. There has been a lot of chatter about the game's "criminal profile" system, which acts similarly to the morality system in the Red Dead Redemption games. In a new video, TGG broke down the different levels of the game's criminal profile system, noting that there are four states: Professional (the highest and most honorable part of the meter), Aggressive, Violent, and the lowest option, Psycho.

There's also an additional unnamed state which will begin to crack and eventually shatter if you are going too far off the rails. Rockstar suggested to TGG that achieving this state is very difficult, and it's partially there for players who clearly demonstrate that they don't care about this system, making it so the game will no longer measure your actions if the meter shatters.

Rockstar is trying to find a balance where players don't have to engage with every system in GTA 6. If you want to kill everyone you see, you can do that without feeling like you're being punished. You can turn off notifications that alert you to your criminal profile's status, allowing you to be blissfully ignorant about how the game views your actions.

The system is more to measure the kind of criminal you are. It measures if your actions are justified. If you're holding up a store and someone shoots back at you, you have the right to kill them without it impacting your criminal profile negatively. However, if you run in and shoot a helpless store clerk or escalate a situation without cause, that's when the meter will begin to slide toward the darker side.

Additionally, Jason and Lucia have their own independent profiles, meaning you can play them completely differently if you want. It's unclear how much this profile will impact the story or if it can change the ending like Red Dead Redemption 2's honor system. Given Rockstar is giving players the freedom to engage with it at all, it's hard to say if it will have a significant impact on how the narrative unravels.

GTA 6 also features a relationship meter, which measures how in love Jason and Lucia are based on the player's actions. This has caused some discourse and controversy on social media among the spouses of players, as they fear they will pay more attention to their in-game partner than their real one. Do what you will with that information.

Ultimately, GTA 6 sounds like a very rich roleplaying experience. It'll be interesting to see just how deep all of these systems go, but it sounds like it has the potential to be one of the most interactive and nuanced games of the generation.

Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

items.title: Resident Evil Movie Popcorn Bucket Is an Organ Transplant Bag
items.description: The official new Resident Evil movie popcorn bucket is styled to look like an organ transplant bag, marking one of the horror franchise's most unsettling collectibles.
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
The popcorn bucket for director Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil movie has been revealed and it’s in the form of an organ transplant bag.

Exhibitors AMC Theaters and Regal Cinemas both posted images of the popcorn bucket, er, bag to their respective social media feeds Tuesday when announcing that tickets are now on sale for the video game movie adaptation.

“One Job: Deliver the Popcorn! See RESIDENT EVIL and purchase our concession collectible starting 9/17, available in theatres only while supplies last,” AMC wrote.

Not to be outdone, Regal posted: “Need a transplant? We recommend this popcorn bag 🫀🍿 Get your hands on the Resident Evil Organ Transplant Popcorn Bag when you see Resident Evil at Regal.”

One Job: Deliver the Popcorn! See RESIDENT EVIL and purchase our concession collectible starting 9/17, available in theatres only while supplies last. Get tickets: https://t.co/jfa32oh6Tl pic.twitter.com/Pvef8AK3H4

— AMC Theatres (@AMCTheatres) September 1, 2026

Need a transplant? We recommend this popcorn bag 🫀🍿

Get your hands on the Resident Evil Organ Transplant Popcorn Bag when you see Resident Evil at Regal. Tickets are on sale now: https://t.co/vqcCWmIw27 pic.twitter.com/x8J4grtVsk

— Regal (@RegalMovies) September 1, 2026

The popcorn bag reveal comes on the heels today of Sony’s release of a new poster for Resident Evil.

Weapons and Barbarian director Zach Cregger has been busy promoting Resident Evil with his main actor Austin Abrams. Cregger recently revealed that Abrams nearly died while they were shooting one particular zombie scene.

The filmmaker also conceded that he “took liberties” to make his movie better even though he knows Resident Evil 2, the game his film is inspired by, didn’t have snow or iPhones in it.

Cregger has also confirmed that his Resident Evil contains first-person sequences and that the games’ sinister Umbrella Corp. is indeed referenced in the film.

Hitting theaters on September 18, Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil is on track to have the biggest opening weekend of any movie in the Resident Evil film franchise.

items.title: Christopher Judge Physically Prepared to Play Kratos in Live-Action God of War Series, but Backed Down for This Reason
items.description: Christopher Judge revealed that he actually started physically preparing to play Kratos in Prime Video’s live-action God of War series before he made himself back down.
items.author: Virginia Glaze
items.content:
Christopher Judge revealed that he actually started physically preparing to play Kratos in Prime Video’s live-action God of War series before he made himself back down.

Speaking on a panel at Fan Expo Canada, Judge said he began working out to get in Spartan shape and started memorizing his lines, admitting that he’d been in talks to take the role in the project’s early days.

"We had talked, and I thought, 'God, what a great legacy to leave for my grandson.' So I started working out. I got bigger,” he began.

“Then, just the reality of it... because I did read! I did read for it. It was so hard for me to memorize my lines, which I never had a problem with. And that was my mind and body starting to tell me, 'You don't want to do this.' I was one of the leads of Stargate at 33 to 44, and then stopped. Now, at 62, to be the lead, I just have no desire to live that way again."

As noted by Collider, Judge previously mentioned the physical toll that such a part would have taken on him. “I didn't want to do it," he said. “I didn't want to, at 62 years old, work 16-to-18-hour days. I didn't want to be dieting constantly; I didn't want to be working out constantly."

That being said, Judge is more than happy for Dave Bautista to take the part, though he is concerned about the pro wrestler-turned-actor getting shredded again after losing so much weight in recent years. He also shared his reaction to Ryan Hurst initially getting cast for the role, saying he felt the actor was a perfect choice due to his history with the God of War games.

“With Ryan, I thought that was absolutely the right choice. He's played all the games. He's a gamer and new father; like, who better? Then when he got hurt, it was like, are they going to take time to read with and call people back? So when I heard the name of Bautista, I thought, 'Didn't he just lose like 100 pounds?' So I hope he's going to be great. I think he's going to be great. I just hope it doesn't cause any health issues to put back on all that weight,” he said.

Prime Video’s God of War series suffered a major setback in July when Hurst tore his bicep filming a stunt for the show. Rather than wait out his lengthy recovery, Amazon decided to recast the role to Dave Bautista in one of the best castings we’ve ever seen for a game adaptation.

While fans balked at the first look we got at the show back in February, responses are looking more positive now that this news has been revealed, alongside a newer photo that Hurst shared of himself in full Kratos makeup that looked far better than the initial poster.

Judge previously criticized Prime Video's God of War series back in August, slamming showrunners for not involving the writers of the 2018 game it's based on (though, in this panel, he clarified that he wants "anything God of War to be great").
